title: Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018
short_title: Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: The Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018 proposes ending live sheep exports to the Middle East over five years, with a summer ban from July to September 2019, citing animal cruelty and scientific evidence. The bill aims to transition to chilled lamb and mutton exports, providing time for farmers and industry to adjust.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: The Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018 would immediately end the northern summer live sheep trade and phase out the remaining trade over five years, citing animal welfare flaws, externalised costs, and shifting consumer preferences. The government pulled its own live export penalty bill from the legislative agenda to avoid amendments, resisting the will of the House.

speeches.speaker: John Alexander
speeches.brief: The member opposed an immediate ban on live sheep exports, arguing instead for a five‑year transition period and noting that 94% of sheep are already processed domestically, with growing frozen export markets. He also welcomed the government’s acceptance of all recommendations from the McCarthy review.

speeches.speaker: Rick Wilson
speeches.brief: The member opposed the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, arguing it would harm farmers, truck drivers and related industries; noted the live export trade is worth $250 million annually with 85% from WA; and stated that mortalities have fallen to 0.7% per voyage from 1.9% in the 1990s, while the 2011 shutdown caused sheep prices to drop from $80–$100 per head to $5 per head and led to suicides.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, citing over 1,600 constituent emails and 4,800 total emails expressing distress, and criticised the government for ignoring the McCarthy review and veterinary advice while calling for a vote and a transition plan for the industry.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for an immediate ban on live sheep exports during the northern summer months and a longer-term phase-out, citing over 2,000 constituent emails and evidence of extreme heat stress, and noted Labor's support for the bill along with a transition plan for farmers.

speeches.speaker: Brian Mitchell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the live sheep export trade is inevitably ending due to unacceptable animal welfare standards, noting that a Liberal MP introduced the prohibition bill. Labor will phase out the trade if elected, with particular attention needed for Western Australian farmers whose business models depend on it.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speech argued for phasing out long-haul live sheep exports over five years, with an immediate ban on summer exports to the Middle East, citing the industry's $250 million value against a $5.23 billion sheepmeat sector and examples like the Thomas Foods facility in Lobethal and proposed abattoirs in Normanville and Kangaroo Island.

speeches.speaker: Jason Wood
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, citing routine animal suffering on 21-day voyages to the Middle East, and recommended independent vets on ships, a ban on exports from May to October, and a transition plan for farmers. They noted government changes announced on 17 May 2018—including 39% more space per sheep and 10-year jail terms for non-compliant directors—but said these are insufficient.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the government's legislative approach over the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, citing the McCarthy review's 23 accepted recommendations, reduced stocking densities (up to 28% reduction), and the industry's $1.4 billion value and 10,000 jobs, while opposing an outright ban due to economic impacts on rural communities.

speeches.speaker: Steve Georganas
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, arguing that the northern summer sheep trade cannot meet animal welfare standards and that New Zealand successfully phased out live exports while creating onshore jobs. They noted that the live export trade has cost thousands of jobs at facilities like Gepps Cross in South Australia, and that Labor is committed to ending the trade and transitioning to onshore processing.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: A motion was moved to suspend standing orders to fast-track the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018 for passage by 6 pm, and the members for Corangamite and Farrer were accused of taking bribes.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: Moved to suspend standing orders to return the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018 from the Federation Chamber and pass it through all stages by 6 pm that day.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Labor supports the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, which would immediately suspend the trade during northern summer months and phase it out over five years, citing over 1,200 constituent concerns about animal welfare. The speaker criticized the bill's mover and seconder for reportedly abandoning their support and called on them to clarify their position in parliament.

speeches.speaker: Steve Georganas
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for an immediate end to live sheep exports, citing animal cruelty and suffering on long-haul voyages, and proposed processing sheep in Australia to add value before export.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Live Sheep Long Haul Export Prohibition Bill 2018, supporting a transition away from live exports to improve animal welfare and create more Australian jobs, and criticised coalition members who abandoned the bill after receiving promotions. They referenced the 60,000 sheep that suffered on the Awassi Express and named the member for Farrer and member for Corangamite as initial supporters who later abandoned the bill.
